Lessons.Title: Subtraction Algorithms (Part 3)
ExplanationParagraphs: Subtraction Algorithms (Part 3): relate expanded-form subtraction to a more compact written algorithm that records each place-value difference with one digit, and any composed hundred or ten in the appropriate column. The 2021 source lesson does NOT carry the inherited 'PLC Activity' title suffix.

Warm-up — Notice and Wonder: Digits that Disappear (10 minutes). Compare the expanded form 300+20 and the equivalent decomposition 200+120. In expanded form, the decomposed hundred is written as 100, while in compact hundreds/tens digits the 3 becomes 2 and 2 tens becomes 12 tens. Ask students to notice how fewer written zeros still represent exactly the same quantity. Use blocks or diagrams to clarify and teacher-review their ideas.

Activity 1 — A New Subtraction Algorithm (20 minutes). Andre and Clare both start from 528−271. Andre records the hundreds and tens expanded: 500+20+8 becomes 400+120+8, then remove200+70+1 to obtain200+50+7=257. Clare records the same 4 hundreds and 12 tens compactly as 4 and 12 in their respective places, then subtracts2 hundreds,7 tens,1 one. The final difference is 257 in either notation. Partners complete both and explain why one needs summing partial-value terms at the end and the other produces the digits directly.

Activity 2 — Try Clare's Algorithm (15 minutes). Source worked example 538−156=382. Use the compact algorithm for four original student exercises: 691−358=333, 926−584=342, 317−182=135, 492−325=167. Display and explain the decomposition whenever the upper digit is smaller than the lower digit in a place-value column.

For 691−358: 1 one cannot remove8 ones, so trade one ten: 8 tens and11 ones; 11−8=3 ones,8−5=3 tens,6−3=3 hundreds, giving333. For 926−584: tens cannot subtract8 tens from2 tens, so exchange one hundred to get12 tens; 12−8=4 tens and8−5=3 hundreds,8−5=3 hundreds. Final 342.

For 317−182 exchange a hundred for ten tens: 2 hundreds and 11 tens. 7−2=5 ones;11−8=3 tens;2−1=1 hundred, final135. 492−325 needs only ones exchange, 12−5=7 ones,8−2=6 tens,4−3=1 hundred, final167. Check results using inverse addition.

Use MLR8 Discussion Supports sentence frames: 'First, I ... because ...', 'Then, I ... because ...'. Permit partners, manipulatives and teacher interaction. The source describes 528 and 271 as student work to be compared, not as one fixed mandatory pencil-and-paper format.

Lesson synthesis: ask how place-value understanding allows writing fewer digits when an expanded 400 and120 correspond to compact 4 and12 in hundreds/tens columns. Discuss where the sum of decomposed parts is or is not needed.

An independent Edulytics Cool-down uses 804−257=547 with exchanges, rather than copying the publisher original teacher-gated Cool-down or repeating the source 492−325 example. The source PDF is linked; publisher illustrations are not reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Expanded notation and compact algorithm
KeyConcepts.Definition: 400+120+8 and 4 hundreds,12 tens,8 ones express the same number.
KeyConcepts.Rule: The place of a digit determines its value.

KeyConcepts.Title: Trade without changing value
KeyConcepts.Definition: A hundred may be exchanged for ten tens; a ten for ten ones.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Only trade to make an equivalent representation before subtracting.

KeyConcepts.Title: Validate subtraction with inverse addition
KeyConcepts.Definition: A difference plus the subtrahend equals the original minuend.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check each result by adding back the amount removed.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating 12 in the tens position as twelve ones.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The notation means twelve tens, i.e.120.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Identify the column and regroup into8? Actually 12 tens=120, not12 ones.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Taking away 8 ones from1 one without regrouping in691−358.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Subtracting the small ones digit from the larger reverses order.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Dropping a newly decomposed hundred when 926−584.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The hundreds column must decrease from9 to8.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Grading written comparison of Andre and Clare solely from scalar257.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original source explicitly asks for comparing process and final representation.
